turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Howzit, I'm Sister Mahlangu. Before Doctor Pillay comes through, your blood pressure is one thirty-two over eighty-four, and your pulse is seventy-six.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Sharp, sister. Ja, I'm fine, hey. Linda just fusses.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ag, Derek. You're not fine and you know it. Sister, have a look at the tablets, I think the file is wrong.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): The file says amitriptyline ten milligrams at night, for sleep.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, shame, that's old. The clinic put him on twenty-five milligrams. Beige tablets, at night, for the sleep. That's what is in the cupboard.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): I'll flag that the doses don't agree. Any allergies?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. Whatever they give me is fine.
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): Good. Doctor will be here now-now.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Morning. I'm Doctor Pillay. What brings you in today?
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His sleep, doctor, and he's got no energy. Since he lost the job he doesn't take an interest in anything.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Derek, how have you been feeling in yourself these last months?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm fine. Really. Did you see the Proteas on Sunday? What a collapse, hey. I nearly switched the TV off.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): I missed the match. I was asking how you've been feeling, not about the cricket.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Ja. Sorry. The sleep is rubbish, if I'm honest. I just lie there.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's been three months of this. Awake half the night, then flat all day.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Three? Ag, longer than that. Since they retrenched me. More like five months. I can't even tell you the date, March or something, I lose track.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): So we'll call it roughly three to five months, and the exact start stays fuzzy. Tell me what the nights are actually like.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm in bed around eleven, still staring at the ceiling at two. Then I'm awake early anyway. Proper exhausted.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): And your energy through the day?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Empty. Like a bakkie with no diesel. I don't even feel like the cricket anymore, and that used to be my whole Saturday.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have you been eating less than usual?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Depends what's for supper.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): I won't put that down as a firm yes. Do you still get any pleasure from things you used to enjoy?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really, no. A braai doesn't even pull me these days.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Mind you, the little one was over last week and that was different, hey. He's four, plastic bat in the garden, doing the Proteas knee slide. We were in stitches.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Shame, he is a proper little batter, that child.

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Weather was lekker that afternoon, not like this heat. Then the drive back, robots out from the load shedding, Centurion to home took an hour. White bakkie cutting everyone off.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The N1 has been a mess all week. Someone needs to sort those robots.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm telling you, the Springboks fix a lineout quicker than the council fixes a robot. Anyway. Grandchild stole the show.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): He sounds like a character, and the traffic has been rough on everyone. Coming back to you, was there a bereavement as well, or was it the job?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No death, no. Just the job. Long-haul logistics. They retrenched the whole shift, and now I sit at home.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry to hear that. At home it's you and Linda?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, just the two of us. Kids are grown, one in Joburg and one in Durban.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or take a drink?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked. I'll have a beer if there's a braai, but I haven't been to one, so basically nothing these days.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): About the amitriptyline, the one for sleep. Are you taking it every night, as it was prescribed?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Some nights I forget. Or I can't be bothered to get up and fetch it. So, not every night.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I put it next to the bed and half the mornings it's still there. And I'm still sure it's the twenty-five, not that ten in the file.

[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): So it's amitriptyline at night for sleep, the dose is either ten or twenty-five depending who you ask, and some doses are missed. I won't settle the dose today. Any other tablets, anything you've stopped?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing else from a doctor. I tried valerian from the chemist for about a week, then I stopped. Didn't do a thing.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): I need to ask this gently, and it's alright to answer straight. Have you had thoughts of harming yourself, or of not wanting to be here?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not. I would never do that to Linda or the kids. Nothing like that.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's said the same at home. He's low, but not that.

[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that's clear. Let me reflect it back. Poor sleep, lying awake till about two and then up early, energy gone, interest gone, for roughly three to five months since the retrenchment. Appetite we left uncertain. No thoughts of harming yourself. The sleeping tablet is irregular and the strength is disputed.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. That's the size of it. Sorry I came in saying I was fine. Old habit.

[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): No apology needed. I've had a listen to your chest. It's clear, the heart sounds are normal, and there's no swelling at the ankles. You look tired, and the mood is flat once we stay with it.

[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): My working impression is a depressive episode, linked to the retrenchment. I can't fully exclude a low thyroid or anaemia until the bloods are back, so those stay on the differential. I'm not calling it definite today.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So you think it's depression. Are you going to start him on something?

[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): It looks like that, yes, but I don't want to start a tablet today. If you're still this flat when we meet again, we can look at citalopram ten milligrams in the morning. Nausea is common at the start, and it takes a few weeks. Not a script today.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, I'd rather not start anything today. I want to think it over. My brother was on some pill and said he felt weird, but that's his story.

[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fair. Nothing new today. What does help in the meantime is a steady bedtime and wake-up, the phone out of the bedroom, a bit of morning light and a short walk, and ease off the coffee after lunch. If the dark thoughts ever show up, you come straight back or go to casualty, you don't wait for the appointment.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'd like a full blood count and a thyroid test, to close off the physical side. Sister can take them when we're finished.
[SEG0053] person_1 (NURSE): I can do the bloods just now. Two tubes, that's all.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Please. And I'd like to see you again in four weeks, even if you feel a shade better, so we can decide about the tablet properly.
[SEG0055] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Four weeks we can do. Should I carry on with the amitriptyline?
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): Don't change the dose on my account while it's unclear. Bring the box from home next time, or a clear photo of the label, and we'll match it to the file.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, I'll bring the box. Label's a bit faded, mind. That chemist by the mall, the one past the broken robot...
[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): The box is enough, faded label and all. Anything you wanted to ask me?
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): The N1 this morning was a disgrace, three robots down and a bakkie on the shoulder. Took forever.
[SEG0060] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Derek. He asked if you have a question.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. No. No questions. I'm chatting again, sorry.
[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's alright. Book the four weeks at reception on your way, and Sister will take the bloods. If he drops further before then, Linda, don't sit on it.
[SEG0063] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll book it. I'll keep an eye. Thank you, doctor.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, thanks. Sorry about the cricket. We'll see you in four weeks, if the bakkie starts.
[SEG0065] person_1 (NURSE): Come through when you're ready and I'll take those samples.

spec.situation: Adult with poor sleep, low energy and loss of interest for months after a job loss or bereavement; partner or parent speaks for them; patient says 'I'm fine' then partly opens up; denies thoughts of self-harm clearly (doctor asks gently); medication discussed but not started today.
features: patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

bad.reason: Family reports flat all day, but 3 to 5 months duration is not stated by family member.
bad.text: Feeling low and flat during the day (category=psychiatric, status=present, duration=approximately 3 to 5 months, temporality=current, reported_by=family_member, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Duration disagreement supported, but transcript mentions poor sleep/flatness, not explicitly low energy in the disagreement.
bad.text: The family member says the poor sleep and flatness have lasted three months, while the patient says about five months since the retrenchment. (type=duration_disagreement, related_entities=symptoms[0]; symptoms[1]; symptoms[3], resolution_status=partially_resolved)

omissions.text: Amitriptyline dose details are missing from the medication entry: the file says 10 mg at night for sleep, while the family member says the clinic changed it to 25 mg at night.
Amitriptyline adherence is incompletely captured under medications: the patient is not taking it every night, sometimes forgets or cannot be bothered to fetch it.
The patient denied smoking and reported essentially no current alcohol intake, saying he only has a beer at a braai and has had basically nothing lately.
Possible reduced appetite was specifically asked about and left uncertain rather than confirmed; the doctor said he would not record it as a firm yes.
There is a preserved enjoyment exception despite overall loss of interest: he did enjoy time with his 4-year-old grandchild last week.
A further denied finding was recorded by the patient: no other prescribed tablets and no other doctor-prescribed medication besides amitriptyline.
The patient preferred not to start any new medication today and wanted to think it over; this aligns with the doctor not prescribing citalopram today.
The doctor gave a safety-net instruction beyond self-harm thoughts alone: if he drops further before the four-week review, Linda should not sit on it.
The planned blood tests were to be taken immediately after the consultation by the nurse ('just now', two tubes).
